result.summary: Discord rouses the Achaeans at dawn and Agamemnon arms and goes on a killing spree until Coon wounds him and he leaves the field. Hector, empowered by Jove, drives the Achaeans back until Diomed, Ulysses, Ajax and others are wounded or pushed back. Nestor carries the wounded Machaon off, and Patroclus, sent by Achilles to ask who is hurt, hears Nestor's long speech and then tends the wounded Eurypylus.

scenes.title: Discord rouses the host
scenes.summary: Jove sends Discord to the ships, Agamemnon arms in splendid armour, and both armies meet while the gods hold aloof.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans face a day of slaughter as Jove plans to give victory to the Trojans.

scenes.title: Agamemnon's rampage
scenes.summary: Agamemnon kills Bienor, Oileus, Isus, Antiphus, Pisander and Hippolochus and chases the Trojans to the Scaean gates.
scenes.stakes: The Trojans risk rout and death, while Agamemnon is pressing close to the city walls.

scenes.title: Jove's message; Agamemnon wounded
scenes.summary: Jove sends Iris to tell Hector to wait until Agamemnon is wounded. Agamemnon kills Iphidamas and Coon but is wounded and leaves, whereupon Hector surges forward.
scenes.stakes: Agamemnon risks his life and the Achaean line once he withdraws; Hector is given a day of triumph.

scenes.title: Diomed, Ulysses and Ajax hold
scenes.summary: Ulysses and Diomed check Hector until Paris wounds Diomed. Ulysses, left alone, is wounded by Socus but rescued by Menelaus and Ajax.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses could be killed or captured, and the ships fall if the line breaks.

scenes.title: Machaon wounded; Ajax retreats
scenes.summary: Paris wounds Machaon, and Nestor drives him off. Jove makes Ajax retreat grudgingly, and Paris wounds Eurypylus.
scenes.stakes: Ajax and the physician Machaon are in danger, and the ships are threatened.

scenes.title: Patroclus sent to Nestor's tent
scenes.summary: Achilles watches from his ship and sends Patroclus to learn who is wounded. At Nestor's tent Hecamede serves a mixed drink.
scenes.stakes: Patroclus's errand begins the chain of events leading to his doom.

scenes.title: Nestor's tale of the Elis raid
scenes.summary: Nestor recounts the cattle raid on Elis and the battle with the Epeans, in which Minerva helped Pylos win.
scenes.stakes: As a young man Nestor risked death in his first battle; Pylos risked oppression by the Epeans.

scenes.title: Nestor recalls Peleus' house
scenes.summary: Nestor reminds Patroclus of Menoetius's charge in Phthia and urges him to persuade Achilles, or to fight in his armour.
scenes.stakes: The Achaeans may be destroyed; Nestor's plan puts Patroclus in Achilles' armour.

scenes.title: Patroclus tends Eurypylus
scenes.summary: Patroclus meets the wounded Eurypylus and takes him to his tent, where he cuts out the arrow and dresses the wound.
scenes.stakes: Eurypylus could bleed to death, and Patroclus is delayed in delivering his message.

alias_notes.explanation: Another name for Paris, husband of Helen.

notable_quotes.reason: Grim image of Agamemnon's brutality as he rolls a severed head like a ball.
Ulysses' resolve: a hero must stand firm whether he wounds or is wounded.
Narrator foreshadows Patroclus' doom, linking this errand to his death.

analysis.text: Jove's plan to honour Achilles by giving Hector victory unfolds as the Achaean leaders fall wounded one after another.
Nestor's speeches use memories of past glory to pressure Patroclus, setting up his entering battle in Achilles' armour.

legacy.text: Nestor's long reminiscences made his name proverbial for a garrulous but wise old counsellor.

fun_facts.text: Agamemnon's detailed arming scene is a typical Homeric 'arming of the hero' type scene, and its description of the breastplate's cyanus is often discussed by scholars of Mycenaean metalwork.

language_notes.text: Tithonus was a Trojan prince loved by Dawn; she won him immortality but not eternal youth, so he withered with age.
Greaves are armour plates protecting the shins; guest-gift means a present exchanged between host and guest.
Cyanus is a dark blue substance, probably an enamel or glass paste, used for inlay in the armour.
Rout and Panic are personified spirits of battlefield flight and terror.
Redoubtable means formidable, inspiring fear.
Dew falling red with blood is a portent, a divine sign of coming slaughter.
"Waxed" means grew; the day was growing toward noon. "Nigh" means near.
A visor here is the front of a helmet protecting the face; it failed to stop the spear.
"Shirts" means the tunics worn under armour; the victors stripped armour and clothing as spoils.
"Withes" are flexible twigs or branches used as bindings.
Antimachus took Alexandrus's (Paris's) bribe to oppose returning Helen, whose abduction caused the war.
Menelaus and Ulysses had come to Troy as envoys to demand Helen's return; Antimachus urged killing them.
"Smite" means strike down or kill with a blow.
"Bedrabbled" means splashed and soiled; here, with blood.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously; here Jove promises to give Hector strength as a favour.
"Bear the brunt" means to take the main force of the attack; Hector is to hold back and let others fight.
Epic poets traditionally invoke the Muses, goddesses of memory and song, when about to recount a long or difficult catalogue of events.
"Cuirass" is body armour covering the chest and back; the girdle is the belt worn beneath it.
"A sleep as it were of bronze" is a poetic phrase for death, linking the sleep to the bronze weapons that killed him.
The Eilithuiae were Greek goddesses who presided over childbirth and its pains; here Juno (the Greek Hera) is their mother.
"Danaans" and "Argives" are alternative names for the Greeks, as is "Achaeans."
"Pell-mell" means in headlong disorder, everyone rushing in confusion.
"Bronze was turned by bronze" means the spear's bronze head glanced off Hector's bronze helmet.
"Ween" is archaic for "think" or "suppose"; Diomed sarcastically presumes Hector prays to Apollo.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen caused the war.
Hades is the god of the dead and the underworld; "yielding your soul to Hades" means dying.
Closing the eyes of the dead was a family duty; being left unburied to vultures was a dreaded dishonour.
Alexandrus is another name for Paris, the Trojan prince who carried off Helen.
"Shepherd of his people" is a stock title for a leader; here it describes Machaon.
"Nothing loth" means not unwilling, so the horses ran eagerly.
"Pell-mell" means in disordered, headlong confusion.
"Tyres" are the metal rims of the wheels; "the rail round the car" is the chariot's rim.
Throwing the shield behind him means slinging it on his back, as a man does when he gives up fighting and turns away.
"He is too many for them" means the ass is too stubborn and strong for the boys to overcome.
"Danaans" and "Argives" are other names for the Achaeans, the Greeks.
The narrator hints that Patroclus's going out now begins the chain of events leading to his death at Hector's hands.
"Man after my own heart" renders a phrase of affection: Patroclus is dear and close to Achilles' spirit.
An esquire is an attendant or squire who serves a warrior, here looking after the horses.
Tenedos is a small island near Troy; Achilles raided it earlier in the war, and Hecamede was part of the spoils given to Nestor.
A "mess" here means a prepared dish or mixture, in this case a thick drink of wine, cheese and barley.
Cyanus is a dark blue material, perhaps enamel or glass paste, used to decorate the table's feet.
Pramnian wine is a strong wine of uncertain origin, mentioned in Homer as the base of this barley drink.
"Recks not" means "pays no heed to"; "reck" is an archaic verb meaning to care or take account of.
"Ruth" is an old word for pity or compassion; "knows no ruth" means he is pitiless.
A "dart" here is a light throwing spear, javelin.
"Chattels" are movable possessions, here goods and livestock owed as repayment.
"To wit" means "that is to say"; it introduces the specific debt, four prize-winning horses.
"Bade" is the past tense of "bid" here, meaning "commanded" or "told".
"Panoply" means a warrior's complete set of armour and equipment.
"Beleaguering" means besieging, surrounding a city to force its surrender.
The Moliones were fathered by Neptune (the Greek Poseidon), though called sons of Actor, their mortal stepfather; hence "their real father."
"Beating up recruits" means rallying and gathering men for the expedition against Troy; Achaea here means Greece generally.
"Straitly" is archaic for strictly or earnestly; the old men gave many solemn instructions.
"Outvie" means to surpass or excel; Peleus urges Achilles to be better than his peers.
Achilles' mother Thetis had told him he had a choice of fates: a short glorious life or a long obscure one; Nestor guesses at a prophecy.
"Descendant of Aeacus" is a patronymic: Achilles' father Peleus was the son of Aeacus.
"Place of assembly and court of justice" means the open space in the camp where the Achaeans met and settled disputes, set beside Ulysses' ships in the middle of the line.
"Feed the hounds of Troy with your fat" means their unburied bodies will be eaten by dogs, a dreaded fate in Homeric warfare.
Chiron was the wise centaur who taught Achilles, and also Aesculapius, the healer, and so passed on knowledge of herbs.
Podalirius and Machaon are sons of the healer Aesculapius and serve as the army's physicians. Machaon was wounded earlier in this book.
"Bulwark of the Achaeans" is a stock epithet for Nestor, calling him a defensive wall for the army.

context_notes.text: Cinyras, king of Cyprus, gave the breastplate to win Agamemnon's favour, hoping to avoid being attacked by the expedition.
Juno and Minerva (the Greek Hera and Athena) favour the Achaeans and honour Agamemnon, king of Mycene.
Polydamas, Aeneas and the sons of Antenor are leading Trojan warriors gathered around Hector.
Priam was king of Troy; his many sons included children born outside marriage.
Ida is the mountain near Troy. Achilles raided the region earlier in the war and ransomed captives.
Jove (the Greek Zeus) removes Hector from battle so Agamemnon can have his moment of glory.
The Scaean gates were the main gates of Troy's walls, facing the plain.
Ida is the mountain near Troy from which Jove watches the battle, and its many springs give it its epithet.
Iris is the gods' messenger, often associated with the rainbow; she regularly carries Jove's commands.
Thrace lay to the north of Greece and was known for horses and sheep; Antenor was a Trojan elder.
Iphidamas leaves his bride immediately after marrying, to fight for Troy, which makes his death all the more pitiful.
The long list of victims is typical of epic battle narrative, giving the slain names and honouring them briefly.
The son of Saturn is Jove (Zeus), who watches the battle from Mount Ida near Troy.
Diomed scorns Paris as an archer; the bow was seen as a less manly weapon than spear and close combat.
Pallas Minerva (Athena) is Ulysses' divine protector throughout the epic.
Skilled healers were rare and highly valued in the Greek army, which is why Machaon must be saved.
Aesculapius (Asclepius) was the famous healer later worshipped as a god of medicine; his sons Machaon and Podalirius served as army physicians.
Hector avoids Ajax, the greatest Achaean fighter in Achilles' absence, because Jove has not granted him victory over him.
Mars is the Roman name for the war god, here used by the translator for the Greek Ares.
Machaon, son of Aesculapius, is a healer among the Achaeans, so his wounding is a serious loss to the army.
Captive women like Hecamede were awarded as prizes of war, a common practice in the poem.
Nestor, the aged king of Pylos, often recalls his youthful exploits to encourage or advise younger warriors.
Hercules (the Greek Heracles) had earlier sacked Pylos and killed Neleus' sons, which explains Pylos' weakness.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) is goddess of war and wisdom, and often aids Greek heroes in battle.
Menoetius is Patroclus' father; Patroclus was raised in Peleus' house after exile and became Achilles' close companion.
Burning thigh-bones wrapped in fat for Jove (the Greek Zeus) was the standard Greek sacrifice; the worshippers then ate the meat.
The Myrmidons are Achilles' own soldiers from Phthia, who have stayed idle at the ships during his quarrel with Agamemnon.
Patroclus is Achilles' closest companion, son of Menoetius. Achilles stays out of the fighting after his quarrel with Agamemnon, and Patroclus is on an errand from Nestor.
Bullock-skins serve as a simple bed in the hut. Patroclus is in Achilles' camp, where he has the herbs to treat wounds.

literary_notes.text: The serpents' arching colours are compared to rainbows, a divine sign, lending the armour a marvellous, omen-like quality.
Hector is likened to a baleful star flickering through clouds, suggesting his ominous, fitful presence in the ranks.
Reapers cutting grain illustrate the steady, even slaughter as both armies cut each other down.
The time of battle is told through a woodcutter's tiredness and hunger, setting ordinary labor beside war.
Agamemnon is a lion and the sons of Priam helpless fawns; the hind's useless terror mirrors the Trojans' inability to help.
Agamemnon turns the father's cruelty into the sons' punishment, ignoring their plea for ransom as Antimachus had denied mercy to envoys.
Comparing the severed head to a ball is grimly casual, showing Agamemnon's brutality.
Forest fire conveys Agamemnon's spreading, unstoppable destruction.
The dead are said to be more useful to vultures than to their wives, a bitter, mocking note.
The spear turning aside "as though it had been lead" and Agamemnon's lion-like fury convey the armour's strength and his ferocity.
The detail of the unenjoyed bride and the cattle paid for her makes Iphidamas's death poignant.
Comparing Agamemnon's wound pain to a woman's labour pangs conveys its sharpness through a surprising, domestic image.
Hector is likened to a huntsman urging hounds against a lion or boar, showing him as a leader driving his men onward.
Hector's charge is compared to a tempest lashing the sea, suggesting overwhelming and unstoppable force.
The west wind scattering clouds and raising waves pictures the Greek dead falling thick and fast before Hector.
The two heroes are compared to wild boars turning on hounds, conveying their fury and their shift from retreat to attack.
Paris's boasting laughter and ambush from behind a pillar show him as a taunting, unheroic fighter.
Ulysses is now the boar surrounded by hunters, reversing the earlier image and stressing his lone, fierce stand.
The wounded stag, jackals and rescuing lion map onto Ulysses, the Trojans and Ajax, foreshadowing his rescue.
Ajax's rampage is likened to a flooding torrent sweeping away oaks and pines, suggesting irresistible, destructive force.
Jove directly puts fear into Ajax, explaining his retreat as the will of the gods rather than cowardice.
Ajax is likened to a lion driven from a farmyard, showing his fierce reluctance and the persistence of his attackers.
The stubborn ass comparison shows Ajax slowly yielding and impossible to hurt, contrasting with the lion image.
Compact comparison to flaming fire conveys the fierce, spreading intensity of the Achaean defence.
The narrator openly warns that this errand starts the misfortune that will destroy Patroclus.
Achilles expects the Achaeans to beg at his knees, but his curiosity sets in motion the tragedy he does not foresee.
Nestor's easy lifting of the heavy cup shows his remarkable strength despite his great age.
Patroclus's description shows Achilles as proud, quick to blame and feared even by his friend.
Nestor's question expresses bitter reproach, pressing Achilles to see the disaster his absence may cause.
Comparing himself to a whirlwind conveys Nestor's speed and destructive force in battle.
Ending with thanks "among mortal men to Nestor" shows his pride and his habit of self-glorifying reminiscence.
Nestor predicts Achilles will bitterly regret his withdrawal, anticipating the heavy Greek losses and Patroclus' death later in the poem.
Menoetius' words define the pair: Achilles is stronger and nobler, Patroclus older and wiser, explaining Patroclus' role as Achilles' counsellor.
The armour plan seems a clever stratagem, but it leads directly to Patroclus' death wearing Achilles' armour.
"Sweat rained" compares dripping sweat to rain, showing how hard Eurypylus has been pushed. His clear mind shows his toughness.
Eurypylus is wounded yet speaks as a clear-headed soldier and reports the grim state of the army without softening it.
